title: Tokens and Text Preparation · Level 1
slo: Prepare text for analysis by using tokenization and common preprocessing methods.

exercises.question_text: What is a corpus in NLP?

options.text: A body of text for analysis
options.rationale: A corpus is the body of language content being analyzed. It is the starting collection before it is broken into tokens.
Normalization can change punctuation or letter case before tokens are generated. It does not define the full body of content being analyzed.
options.better_fit: This fits when describing content after surface differences have been standardized.

feedback.intrinsic: You would mistake a preparation result for the full collection of content.
feedback.instructional: A corpus is the whole body of content; normalization is only one possible preparation step.

options.rationale: A sequence of terms treated as one group is an n-gram. A corpus can contain many such sequences.
options.better_fit: This fits when naming a phrase such as a two-word bigram or three-word trigram.

feedback.intrinsic: You would label one small phrase as though it were the entire collection.
feedback.instructional: An n-gram is a grouped sequence of terms, while a corpus is the body of content under analysis.

options.text: A grammatical label for a word
options.rationale: A grammatical label such as noun or verb comes from POS tagging. It describes an individual token, not the collection being analyzed.
options.better_fit: This fits when identifying a token’s grammatical category.

feedback.intrinsic: You would focus on one token’s grammar instead of the collection to prepare.
feedback.instructional: POS tagging labels tokens; a corpus is the body of content containing those tokens.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A corpus is the body of content selected for analysis.

exercises.question_text: Which statements about n-grams are correct? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: A unigram is a one-word phrase treated as a group. It is the one-term form of an n-gram.
A bigram is a sequence of two terms treated as a group. Multi-term groups can preserve phrase meaning.
A trigram has three words. A two-word sequence is a bigram.
options.better_fit: This fits if “trigram” is replaced with “bigram.”

feedback.intrinsic: You would assign the wrong group size to a phrase.
feedback.instructional: Remember the counts: unigram is one, bigram is two, and trigram is three.

options.rationale: Removing endings such as “ing” and “ed” is stemming. An n-gram groups a sequence of terms.

feedback.intrinsic: You would change word forms instead of preserving a meaningful sequence.
feedback.instructional: N-grams group terms; stemming strips endings to consolidate related forms.

exercises.explanation: Correct. N-grams are grouped sequences, and their names indicate the number of terms.

exercises.question_text: Tokenization can create tokens from whole words, partial words, or combinations of words and punctuation.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Treating tokens as words only can miss how punctuation and word parts are represented.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Tokenization can produce whole words, partial words, or combinations of words and punctuation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Tokens are not limited to whole words.

exercises.question_text: A bigram is a sequence of three terms treated as a group.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Using three terms would place the phrase in the wrong n-gram category.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A unigram has one word, a bigram has two, and a trigram has three.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A bigram has two terms.

exercises.question_text: Which method strips endings such as “ing” and “ed” to group related forms?

options.rationale: Stemming strips endings such as “s,” “ing,” and “ed.” It consolidates related forms under a shared root.
Lemmatization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to return a valid dictionary base form. It does more than simply chop endings.
options.better_fit: This fits when a valid lemma such as “run” is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: You might expect a valid dictionary form when only ending stripping is being described.
feedback.instructional: Stemming strips endings; lemmatization uses rules and vocabulary to produce a valid word.

options.rationale: Normalization can lowercase words or remove punctuation. It does not strip endings to group related forms.
options.better_fit: This fits when standardizing case or punctuation before token generation.

feedback.intrinsic: Related forms could remain separate during counting.
feedback.instructional: Use stemming to consolidate endings such as “ing” and “ed”; normalization handles surface differences.

options.rationale: POS tagging labels a token as a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb. It does not alter word endings.
options.better_fit: This fits when grammatical categories are required.

feedback.intrinsic: You would add grammar labels without grouping the related word forms.
feedback.instructional: POS tagging classifies grammar; stemming strips endings.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Stemming groups related forms by stripping endings.

exercises.question_text: Which actions are text normalization? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Removing punctuation is a surface-form standardization. It can help analysis based purely on word frequency.
Changing case standardizes surface differences before token generation. This can improve frequency-based analysis.

options.error_type: Confuses normalization with stop word removal
options.rationale: Excluding common words is stop word removal. Normalization instead standardizes features such as punctuation and capitalization.
options.better_fit: This fits when low-meaning common words should be removed to reveal content words.

feedback.intrinsic: You would remove words rather than standardize their surface form.
feedback.instructional: Stop word removal excludes words like “the”; normalization can lowercase words or remove punctuation.

options.text: Use grammar rules for base forms
options.rationale: Using linguistic rules and vocabulary to produce a valid base form is lemmatization. Normalization does not perform that dictionary-form reduction.
options.better_fit: This fits when a valid lemma such as “run” is required.

feedback.intrinsic: You would change word forms when the task only calls for surface standardization.
feedback.instructional: Lemmatization uses rules and vocabulary; normalization handles case and punctuation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Both actions standardize surface differences before token generation.

exercises.question_text: POS tagging can label a token as a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb by using the token and its context.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Ignoring context can lead to the wrong grammatical category for a token.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: POS tagging labels tokens as noun, verb, adjective, or adverb and uses both the token and its sentence context.

exercises.explanation: Correct. POS tagging assigns grammatical categories using the token and its context.

exercises.question_text: Which word is a common stop word?

options.rationale: “The” is a common word that helps people read but often adds little semantic meaning. It is a standard stop-word example.
This is a two-term phrase that can be treated as a bigram. It is not a common low-meaning word.
options.better_fit: This fits when identifying a meaningful two-word n-gram.

feedback.intrinsic: You would remove a phrase that may identify a main topic.
feedback.instructional: Stop words are common words such as “the,” “a,” and “it,” not meaningful multi-term phrases.

options.error_type: Confuses stop words with a word form
options.rationale: “Running” is a word form that can be reduced to “run” by lemmatization. It is not identified as a common stop word.
options.better_fit: This fits when discussing a word that lemmatization can reduce to a valid base form.

feedback.intrinsic: You could remove a content word instead of preparing its form.
feedback.instructional: Stop word removal targets common low-meaning words; “running” is used to illustrate lemmatization.

options.error_type: Confuses stop words with punctuation-sensitive token
options.rationale: “Banks.” may differ from “banks” because the period signals sentence position. It is not a listed common stop word.
options.better_fit: This fits when preserving punctuation-sensitive meaning is important.

feedback.intrinsic: You would discard a token whose punctuation may carry useful meaning.
feedback.instructional: Stop words are common readability words; punctuation-sensitive terms can need to be retained.

exercises.explanation: Correct. “The” often adds little semantic meaning and may be excluded.

exercises.question_text: Text normalization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to return valid dictionary forms.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing true would substitute base-form reduction for surface standardization.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Lemmatization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to return a valid dictionary form. Normalization can lowercase words or remove punctuation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. That process is lemmatization, not normalization.

exercises.question_text: Stop word removal changes every word to lowercase before analysis.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing true would use the wrong preparation method for common-word removal.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Stop word removal excludes words such as “the,” “a,” and “it.” Changing case is text normalization.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Lowercasing is a normalization action.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The timing of the preparation action is no longer clear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Name normalization, state its action, then show that it can happen before tokens are generated.

exercises.correct_answer: Text normalization can remove punctuation before tokens are generated
exercises.explanation: Normalization is a preparation choice that can occur before token generation, so the timing phrase follows the action.

exercises.question_text: Words such as “the,” “a,” and “it” are often called ___.

parts.text: Words such as “the,” “a,” and “it” are often called

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The label would confuse common low-meaning words with units, phrases, or dictionary base forms.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Tokens are units, n-grams are term sequences, and lemmas are valid base forms. “The,” “a,” and “it” are stop words.

exercises.explanation: These common readability words often add little semantic meaning, so they may be excluded to highlight content words.

flashcards.back: It breaks a corpus into tokens.
It standardizes text, such as lowercase words or removed punctuation.
Common words that often add little semantic meaning.
A two-word sequence treated as a group.
